comments.author: @diestormlie
comments.text:
It's important to note that the UK was never occupied and never had a Revolution. There was no great, endurint moment of "Now it is time to rebuild the Governance of this country from the ground up." So really, what we have is essentially a *heavily* reformed Feudal system.

(Well, there was the English Civil War and the Commonwealth of England, but by the end of it we decided to essentially just roll back the clock!)

The concept at play here is that of *Personal Union*. The best modern analogy I can think of is that of someone managing to get elected as the President of two different countries.

Imagine if someone got elected as the President of France and of Germany. They would have the powers of both Presidencies, but one guy sitting on both chairs doesn't magically compel the two to unite into one country.

A more specifically British example: When Elizabeth I died and the English Crown passed to James VI (of Scotland)/James I (of England), Scotland and England did not unity into a single country: They remained seperate countries, with their own armies, navies, laws, Parliaments etc.

The Crown Dependencies are in Personal Union with the crown of the UK: Separate legal entities that just happen to be governed by someone who sits in a different, far more gilded chair.

comments.author: @thesuperj2511
comments.text:
I'm from the UK, but i have had the pleasure of studying Channel Islands law during my degree to quite some depth. You didn't mention a lot of really interesting extra parts about the weird system there so here are a tew.
Firstly, Sark's fiefdom continued quite unchanged up until about 2008, when a couple of billionaires got disgruntled about it affecting their assets when buying an island and basically embarrassed the Crown into reforming a medieval system. The Seigneurs could make any law and receive taxes paid by their subjects for aimply living there. For example, pet birds and unspayed dogs were only allowed to be owned by the Seigneur, and a ban on cars continues to today. Even ambulances must be horse-drawn. The old-world system is so in need of update that it's getting in the way of effectively governing modern issues. It was recently brought to light that children can legally buy cannabis gummies, though no reports of these purchases actually happening have been reported among the very small population.
Norman French is still used a lot in law because old texts before any shift to English began cannot legally be translated for fear of corrupting original meaning, so legal updates to these remain in French too. It also survives in some customs in the parliaments of the islands.
By far the strangest feature has got to be the Clameur de Haro, which is a fully inforceable injunction whereby a 'criant' who believes there is wrongdoing against in relation to private land kneels before the defendant and at least two other witnesses, raises their arm to the sky and recites in French: Hear me!
Hear me! Hear me! Come to my aid, my prince, for someone does me wrong! (Prince referring to a former Viking prince). They must then recite the Lord's prayer in French followed by an additional blessing if you're in Guernsey.
There is a fine to either party if they do not stop what they are doing at that moment and the clameur was legitimate. The parties then sort it out in a court of law. It's rarely used but a recent example was in 2016 when authorities tried to remove a derelict car from someone's land, although I don't think it was successful. Someone also tried it in 2021 to avoid eviction, but by that point it wasn't their private land.

comments.author: @MatthewMcVeagh
comments.text:
Hi Barbs. excellent treatment of the subject. This topic has been tackled in less detail by many past YouTubers, e.g. CGP Grey's well-known account of the relationships of the 'British Isles'. But you've drilled down to the details of how the Crown Dependencies are run and what they call things.

Interesting point for me as a Brit is that if the relationship between the Crown and the Dependencies is feudal, by implication that between the Crown and the UK is equally feudal. And the point about these feudal relationships is that they're an anomaly in the modern world, where countries have generally lost such mediaeval structures, if they ever had them, and replaced them with those of modern states. We might ask why the British monarchy had not lost its feudal relationships to lands and peoples in the same way as the rest of the world. We can see that it took all sorts of revolutions and wars to uproot these older structures in many countries, but it's also the case that there needed to be a will to change on the part of populations or at least political elites. There hasn't been sufficient such will in the British political world at any time since the civil wars of the 1640s. And so we're stuck with the monarchy and all its complicated side projects like the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man.

 Jersey and Guernsey were a part of the Common Travel Area with the UK and Ireland. Work and property permits are independently controlled - so you may be able to visit there without a visa, but you may not be able to live and work there.

comments.text: So what's the difference between Crown Dependancy and Commonwealth Realm? As far as I understand both are sovereign countries that have the British monarch as their head of state

replies.author: @TheEbrithil2
replies.text: ​@LordDim1 wow, thanks for the in-depth explanation. Post-Empire Britain is really complicated

replies.author: @LordDim1
replies.text:
Commonwealth Realms are sovereign, independent states. The Crown Dependencies are not. The Crown Dependencies are under British sovereignty, and thus the UK handles their defence and foreign affairs.

What he described here was the *British* Crown (which covers everything under British sovereignty). The Commonwealth realms (the independent countries where King Charles is head of state, like Canada or Australia) each have their own Crown, which is its own separate sovereign entity from the British Crown. Canada is under the Canadian Crown, while Australia is under the Australian Crown, etc. Legally and constitutionally, these Crowns are all completely separate, distinct and unrelated entities, it just so happens that the same person “wears” each of these crowns at the same time.

This is what separates the Crown Dependencies from the Commonwealth Realms. The dependencies are self governed, but under the British Crown, meaning they are under British sovereignty, while the Commonwealth realms are self governed under their own, distinct Crown, meaning they are under their own sovereignty. In fact, the commonwealth realm crowns can have their own weird dependent territories. The New Zealand Crown has its own analogue to the Crown Dependencies: the Cook Islands and Niue. The Cook Islands and Niue are self-governed, with their own parliaments, constitutions, prime ministers and passports, just like the Crown Dependencies, but they are under the sovereignty of the New Zealand Crown, and therefore New Zealand has responsibility for foreign affairs and defence.
